title: Architectural Boundaries in Practice
summary: Enforcing architectural boundaries in a real, evolving codebase rather than trusting convention, and knowing when the ceremony genuinely isn't worth it.

slides.markdown:
Every boundary this group has covered — layers, ports, aggregate roots, bounded contexts — is a design-time decision. None of them enforce themselves. A codebase that was cleanly layered on the day it launched can, eighteen months and forty engineers later, have a dozen upward imports nobody noticed, because there was never anything stopping the first one.

This closing topic is about the gap between drawing a boundary and keeping it real: how teams enforce boundaries structurally instead of by convention, how boundaries erode when they aren't, and — just as important — how to recognize when a project genuinely doesn't need this much structure in the first place.

slides.sectionTitle: Enforcing boundaries with modules and visibility
slides.subTitle: Not just convention
slides.markdown:
The cheapest, most reliable enforcement is structural: use the language and build system's own visibility rules so that a forbidden import is a compile error, not a code-review catch. Java/Kotlin `internal`/package-private modifiers, Go's lowercase-unexported identifiers and internal packages, Python's `__init__.py`-based package boundaries with linting, or a proper module system (Java Platform Module System, Gradle's project-per-module) can all make "data access imports presentation" physically impossible to compile.

This matters because convention-based enforcement — a wiki page describing the layering rule, a note in the README — degrades under deadline pressure. Nobody sets out to violate the boundary; someone under a Friday-afternoon deadline takes the shortest path to green tests, and the shortest path is often one upward import that a linter would have caught in three seconds but a busy reviewer misses in a 400-line pull request.

slides.subTitle: Automated checks that a boundary rule holds
slides.markdown:
Where a language's own visibility rules aren't granular enough — most real systems eventually have a rule that isn't expressible as a simple module boundary — teams write **architecture tests**, sometimes called **fitness functions**: automated tests that inspect the codebase's dependency graph and fail the build if a forbidden import edge exists.

Concrete tools: **ArchUnit** in Java/Kotlin lets you write `noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..data..").should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..presentation..")` and runs it as a normal unit test in CI. **import-linter** in Python and **dependency-cruiser** in JavaScript/TypeScript do the equivalent by parsing imports and checking them against a declared set of allowed edges.

The advantage over a human review catching this: it runs on every commit, doesn't get tired, and turns "we have a layering convention" into "we have a test that fails the build within seconds if the convention is violated" — the same shift unit tests made for business logic correctness, applied to structure instead of behavior.

Boundary erosion almost never happens as one deliberate decision to break the rule — it happens as a sequence of individually-reasonable-seeming shortcuts, each one slightly widening a crack the last one opened.

The typical sequence: a deadline forces one upward import "just this once, we'll clean it up later." The cleanup never happens, because there's no signal telling anyone it's owed. A second engineer, months later, sees that import already exists in the codebase and reasonably concludes it must be an allowed pattern, adding a second one. By the time a team notices the erosion — often triggered by an unrelated bug that's hard to trace specifically because logic ended up in the wrong layer — untangling it requires identifying which of dozens of upward imports are load-bearing and which were opportunistic, a much harder problem than it would have been to reject the first one.

The practical implication: enforcement needs to exist *before* the first violation, not after several have accumulated — a fitness function added after erosion has to be introduced alongside a cleanup pass, or it fails immediately on legacy violations that predate it.

slides.sectionTitle: A strictly-enforced boundary vs. a documented-but-unenforced one
slides.markdown:
| | Documented only (README, wiki, onboarding doc) | Enforced (module boundaries / architecture tests) |
|---|---|---|
| **Catches a violation** | Only if a reviewer happens to notice it in a diff | Automatically, on every commit, in CI |
| **Survives team turnover** | Degrades — new engineers may never read the doc | Persists — the rule is executable, not tribal knowledge |
| **Cost to set up** | Near zero — write the doc | Real but one-time — write the module boundaries or the test suite |
| **Cost of a violation slipping through** | Discovered late, often as a confusing bug, expensive to unwind | Build fails immediately, cheap to fix at the commit that caused it |

Documentation isn't worthless — it explains *why* the rule exists, which a failing test can't do on its own. The two are complementary: docs for the reasoning, enforcement for the guarantee.

slides.subTitle: A CRUD admin tool doesn't need four layers
slides.markdown:
Everything in this group has a real cost: extra files, extra indirection, a wiring step, a slower "where does this go" decision for every new piece of code. That cost is worth paying when there's real business complexity to protect from the framework and the database. It is not automatically worth paying for every project.

A useful heuristic: ask how much of the system's value is in its **business rules** versus its **plumbing**. An internal admin tool that lets support staff edit a database row through a form has almost no business rule — it's nearly all plumbing, and a thin single-layer CRUD implementation is not under-engineering, it's correctly matching structure to actual complexity. A pricing engine with dozens of interacting discount rules, eligibility exceptions, and regulatory constraints is nearly all business rule, and skipping the architecture there isn't simplicity, it's accepting that the rules will end up scattered and untestable.

The judgment call gets harder in the middle — most real systems start simple and grow real business logic over time, which is exactly the next slide's topic.

slides.subTitle: The strangler pattern
slides.markdown:
When a system genuinely needs better boundaries than it has — a CRUD app that grew real business complexity, or a monolith with erosion that needs correcting — a full rewrite is rarely the right answer: it freezes feature delivery, and the rewritten system tends to rediscover requirements the original handled via years of small fixes.

The **strangler fig pattern** (named after the vine that grows around a host tree, gradually taking over) is the standard incremental alternative: build the new, better-structured version of one piece alongside the old one, route a slice of real traffic or calls to the new implementation once it's proven correct, and repeat piece by piece until nothing routes to the old code path, which you then delete. At every step the system is fully working — there's no long-lived "big rewrite" branch that has to catch up with months of changes to the code it's replacing.

Applied to layering specifically: introduce the domain-owned interface and one adapter for a single use case first, verify it in production, then migrate the next use case — never a single flag-day cutover of the whole system's boundary structure at once.

slides.sectionTitle: Full Clean Architecture on day one of a startup MVP
slides.markdown:
The mirror-image mistake to boundary erosion: applying the full weight of Clean Architecture's rings, ports, and aggregates to a brand-new MVP whose entire purpose is to test whether the product idea has any customers at all.

The cost here isn't abstract — it's real engineering time spent on interfaces, mappers, and ring boundaries for business rules that may not exist yet, or may be completely different in three months once real usage reveals what the product actually needs to do. Startups in this situation frequently ship slower for a launch that could fail regardless of code quality, and if the product does succeed, the architecture built around week-one assumptions about the domain is often wrong anyway, because nobody understood the real business rules until customers showed up.

The right sequencing in this specific situation is usually the reverse of what feels responsible: ship the thin, simple version first, let the business logic reveal itself through real usage, and introduce boundaries where the resulting complexity actually justifies the cost — which is a judgment call, not a rule, but one worth making deliberately rather than defaulting to maximum structure out of habit.

Putting the group's ideas into one practical sequence for a real project:

1. **Start with plain layering** (presentation / business / data) — it's cheap and it's almost always worth it past a trivial script.
2. **Add dependency inversion at the boundaries that will plausibly change** — the database, a payment provider, an email service. Skip it for genuinely stable, unlikely-to-change dependencies if the ceremony isn't earning its keep yet.
3. **Reach for full hexagonal/Clean Architecture rings** once business logic has real rules worth protecting from frameworks — not before.
4. **Model with DDD's tactical patterns** where consistency actually matters — an aggregate boundary should map to a real invariant, not just "these things feel related."
5. **Draw bounded contexts** once more than one team or subdomain genuinely has a different model of the same concept.
6. **Enforce whatever you land on** with module boundaries or architecture tests, before violations accumulate, not after.

Every step is reversible and additive — none of this requires committing to the heaviest version on day one.

Every idea in this group — layering, dependency inversion, ports and adapters, entities and value objects, aggregates, bounded contexts — answers the same underlying question at a different scale: **what should depend on what, and who gets to change without breaking someone else?**

The patterns are tools, not doctrine. The senior-level skill isn't knowing all of their names — it's knowing which ones a specific system, at its specific size and with its specific business complexity, actually needs right now, and having the discipline to enforce whatever boundary you do draw so it's still there in two years, under a different team, past the deadline that would otherwise have quietly eroded it.
